one_line_takeaway: A taxonomy-driven survey that jointly maps LLM jailbreak attacks (white-box vs. black-box) against defenses (prompt-level vs. model-level) plus their evaluation benchmarks, arguing attacks are getting more transferable and cheaper while defenses lag.
core_contribution: This is a survey paper (Yi et al., Tsinghua/HKUST-GZ). Its own contribution is NOT any new attack or defense but three organizational artifacts: (1) a systematic two-axis taxonomy of jailbreak ATTACKS — split into white-box attacks (gradient-based, logits-based, fine-tuning-based) and black-box attacks (template completion, prompt rewriting, LLM-based generation), each further subdivided (e.g., template completion into scenario nesting, context-based, code injection); and DEFENSES — split into prompt-level (prompt detection, prompt perturbation, system prompt safeguard) and model-level (SFT-based, RLHF-based, gradient/logit analysis, refinement, proxy defense), organized by whether the defense modifies the protected model (Table 1); (2) an explicit mapping of relationships between attack and defense sub-classes (Figure 1), noting a defense built for one attack often generalizes to others; (3) an investigation and comparison of current evaluation methods, metrics, benchmarks/datasets and toolkits. The paper explicitly positions itself against prior surveys (Shayegani et al., Esmradi et al., Rao et al., Geiping et al., Schulhoff et al.) as filling the gap that those did not jointly categorize corresponding DEFENSE techniques.
threat_model: Adversary crafts adversarial prompts (or maliciously fine-tunes) to bypass an aligned LLM's safety guardrails and elicit policy-violating/harmful outputs. Two attacker capability tiers are surveyed: white-box attackers with access to model gradients/logits/weights (enabling gradient-based suffix optimization like GCG, logit manipulation, and fine-tuning attacks), and black-box attackers with query-only access (template/scenario-nesting, cipher and low-resource-language rewriting, genetic-algorithm search, and LLM-driven prompt generation, including transfer from surrogate models). Impacts cited include privacy breaches, misinformation, and manipulation of automated/agentic systems. Defenders correspondingly operate at the prompt level (input filtering/perturbation, system-prompt hardening) or model level (safety SFT/RLHF, gradient/logit analysis, self-refinement, external guard/proxy models).
limitations: As a survey it contributes no new method, dataset, or experiment; all effectiveness numbers are secondhand and not independently reproduced or normalized (different works use different target models, dataset subsets, and success criteria, which the paper itself flags as an unsolved 'what counts as a successful jailbreak' problem). The taxonomy is a snapshot of mid-2024 literature (arXiv v2, Aug 2024) and will date quickly given the fast-moving field. The claimed attack-defense relationship map (Figure 1) is asserted from other papers' experiments rather than validated by the authors. Coverage is breadth-first with brief per-method descriptions, so it is a navigational map rather than a source of deep methodological or quantitative comparison.

datasets_used: Survey compiles/compares 13 evaluation datasets in Table 2 (not used for original experiments): XSTEST (450, EN)
quantitative_results: No original experiments — all figures are cited from surveyed works
AutoDAN highest ASR only ~35% on Llama-2-chat
Fine-tuning with ~340 adversarial examples -> ~95% harmful-output likelihood (dismantles RLHF)
LoRA fine-tuning reduces target refusal rate to <1% (Lermen et al.)
100 harmful examples in <1 GPU hour markedly raises jailbreak susceptibility (Yang et al.)
PANDORA RAG poisoning: 64.3% ASR ChatGPT, 34.8% GPT-4
Kang et al. code-injection: up to 100% filter bypass
Low-resource-language translation raises GPT-4 bypass rate from <1% to 79%
Many-shot in-context: ~80% vs Claude 2.0 at 128 shots; Zheng et al. ~100% on open-source incl. Llama-3
Two formalized metrics: ASR = N_success/N_total (Eq.1), Perplexity PPL (Eq.2)
baselines_compared: No experimental baselines — survey, not an empirical study
Positions itself against 5 prior jailbreak surveys (Shayegani et al., Esmradi et al., Rao et al., Geiping et al., Schulhoff et al.) as the first to jointly taxonomize defenses alongside attacks
Compares evaluation toolkits: JailbreakEval, HarmBench, JailbreakBench, EasyJailbreak, Safety-Prompts platform
